prompt: Which is NOT allowed when drawing a resonance structure?
choices: Moving an atom to a new position
Moving a lone pair into an adjacent bond
Moving a pi bond onto an adjacent atom as a lone pair
Shifting a pi bond one position along a conjugated system
explanation: Only electrons move between resonance forms. If an atom moved, you have drawn a different compound — an isomer, not a resonance structure.
teach: The single rule that catches most mistakes: atoms stay frozen, electrons move.

prompt: For resonance to be possible, the participating orbitals must be:
choices: Aligned in the same plane so their p orbitals overlap side by side
Perpendicular to each other
On atoms that are far apart
All sp3 hybridized
explanation: Delocalization requires continuous p-orbital overlap. Twist the system out of plane and the conjugation breaks.
teach: Resonance needs a conjugated, planar system: alternating p orbitals lined up so electrons can spread across them.

prompt: How many significant resonance structures can be drawn for the carboxylate ion, RCOO⁻?
choices: 2 — equivalent, with the negative charge on either oxygen
explanation: The double bond and the negative charge swap between the two oxygens. Because the forms are equivalent, each oxygen carries −½.
teach: Equivalent resonance forms give maximum stabilization — the reason carboxylic acids are far more acidic than alcohols.

prompt: Which species has NO resonance stabilization?
choices: The ethoxide ion, CH₃CH₂O⁻
The acetate ion, CH₃COO⁻
The phenoxide ion, C₆H₅O⁻
The allyl cation, CH₂=CH–CH₂⁺
explanation: Ethoxide's negative charge sits on an oxygen with only an sp3 carbon beside it — there is no adjacent pi system or empty orbital to delocalize into.
teach: Resonance needs a neighbour to share with: an adjacent pi bond, an adjacent empty orbital, or an adjacent lone pair.

prompt: In the nitro group (–NO₂), the two N–O bonds are experimentally found to be:
choices: Identical in length, intermediate between a single and a double bond
One clearly short and one clearly long
Both full single bonds
Both full triple bonds
explanation: The real molecule is the hybrid, not either drawing. Equivalent resonance forms average out to two identical bonds of intermediate length.
teach: Measured bond lengths are the physical evidence that resonance hybrids are real and the individual structures are not.

prompt: Which carbocation is MOST stabilized by resonance?
choices: The benzylic cation, C₆H₅–CH₂⁺
The tert-butyl cation, (CH₃)₃C⁺
The ethyl cation, CH₃CH₂⁺
The methyl cation, CH₃⁺
explanation: Only the benzylic cation has resonance available: the empty p orbital overlaps with the ring, spreading the charge over four positions. The others rely on hyperconjugation alone.
teach: Ranking cations: resonance-stabilized (benzylic, allylic) beats 3° beats 2° beats 1° beats methyl.

prompt: When two resonance structures are NOT equivalent, the hybrid:
choices: Resembles the more stable structure more closely
Is an exact 50:50 average
Resembles the less stable structure
Is unaffected by their relative stabilities
explanation: Contributors are weighted by stability — the major contributor dominates the hybrid's character.
teach: For an amide, the neutral form is the major contributor, but the charge-separated form contributes enough to make the C–N bond partly double and block rotation.

prompt: Why is an amide's C–N bond unable to rotate freely at room temperature?
choices: Resonance gives it partial double-bond character
The nitrogen is sp3 hybridized
The bond is ionic
Amides are always cyclic
explanation: The nitrogen lone pair delocalizes into the carbonyl, so the C–N bond is part double. Rotating it would break that overlap.
teach: This restricted rotation is what holds proteins' backbone geometry — the peptide bond is an amide.

prompt: Which resonance structure is the LEAST significant contributor?
choices: One with a positive charge on oxygen and a negative charge on carbon
One with no formal charges and full octets
One with a negative charge on oxygen and positive on carbon
One with full octets and adjacent opposite charges
explanation: Putting positive charge on the most electronegative atom and negative charge on carbon fights electronegativity — a very poor contributor.
teach: Negative charge belongs on electronegative atoms; positive charge belongs on the least electronegative. Structures that reverse this contribute little.

prompt: The allyl anion, CH₂=CH–CH₂⁻, has its negative charge:
choices: Shared equally between the two terminal carbons
Localized on the central carbon
Localized on one terminal carbon only
Spread over all three carbons equally
explanation: Two equivalent resonance forms place the charge on either end carbon, so each carries −½. The central carbon carries none.
teach: In allylic systems the charge alternates to the ENDS, never resting on the middle carbon.

prompt: Benzene is drawn as two structures with alternating double bonds. What is the real molecule like?
choices: A single hybrid with six identical C–C bonds, each of intermediate length
Rapidly flipping between the two structures
A mixture of two different compounds
Three short bonds and three long bonds
explanation: Benzene never 'switches' — it is permanently the hybrid, with all six bonds identical (139 pm, between a single 154 and a double 134).
teach: The double-headed arrow means 'is a blend of', not 'turns into'. This is the most common resonance misconception.

prompt: Which group can donate electron density into a benzene ring by resonance?
choices: –OH (it has lone pairs to share)
–CH₃ (it has no lone pairs)
–NO₂ (it withdraws)
–CF₃
explanation: An OH lone pair can push into the ring, enriching it. Methyl donates only weakly by induction and hyperconjugation, having no lone pair to give.
teach: Donation by resonance needs a lone pair adjacent to the pi system. This is the basis of aromatic substitution directing effects later on.

prompt: An enolate forms when an alpha-hydrogen is removed from a carbonyl compound. Its negative charge is shared between:
choices: The alpha carbon and the carbonyl oxygen
Two carbons only
Two oxygens
The carbonyl carbon and its oxygen
explanation: One resonance form puts the charge on carbon, the other on oxygen. The oxygen form is the major contributor, since oxygen holds negative charge better.
teach: This dual character makes enolates react at either site — a central theme of carbonyl chemistry.

prompt: Which pair of drawings does NOT show a valid resonance relationship?
choices: Two structures where a hydrogen has moved to a neighbouring atom
Two structures where a pi bond has shifted along a conjugated chain
Two structures where a lone pair became a pi bond
Two structures where a pi bond became a lone pair
explanation: Moving a hydrogen moves an ATOM. Those two drawings are tautomers — genuinely different compounds in equilibrium — not resonance forms.
teach: Tautomers use an equilibrium arrow (⇌) and are separate species; resonance forms use ↔ and describe one species.

prompt: Resonance stabilization makes a conjugate base MORE stable. What does that do to the acidity of its conjugate acid?
choices: Increases acidity — a more stable conjugate base means a stronger acid
Decreases acidity
Has no effect on acidity
Makes the acid neutral
explanation: Anything stabilizing the deprotonated form makes losing the proton more favorable, lowering pKa.
teach: This single idea explains most pKa comparisons in orgo: carboxylic acid (4.8) beats phenol (10) beats alcohol (16), tracking how well each conjugate base delocalizes.

prompt: For a lone pair to participate in resonance with an adjacent pi bond, the atom holding it should be:
choices: In a p orbital aligned with the pi system, which usually means the atom becomes sp2
sp3 hybridized with the lone pair pointing away
Positively charged
A hydrogen atom
explanation: The lone pair must sit in an unhybridized p orbital parallel to the pi system. Atoms often rehybridize to sp2 to make that possible — as amide nitrogen does.
teach: This is why the amide nitrogen is planar and sp2 even though counting groups suggests sp3.

prompt: Which explains why phenol (pKa ≈ 10) is far more acidic than cyclohexanol (pKa ≈ 16)?
choices: Phenoxide delocalizes its negative charge into the aromatic ring; cyclohexanol's alkoxide cannot delocalize at all
Phenol has more carbons
Cyclohexanol contains a ring and phenol does not
Phenol's O–H bond is ionic
explanation: Phenoxide spreads its charge onto three ring carbons; cyclohexanol's alkoxide keeps it entirely on one oxygen.
teach: Six orders of magnitude in acidity from resonance alone — a good measure of how much delocalization is worth.

prompt: A structure where every atom has a full octet but there are +1 and −1 charges on adjacent atoms is:
choices: A legitimate but minor contributor — acceptable, though less important than a neutral full-octet form
Never allowed
Always the major contributor
Not a resonance structure at all
explanation: Charge separation costs energy, so such a form contributes less than a neutral one — but it is valid and often matters, as in the amide.
teach: Ranking order: full octets first, then fewest charges, then charges on the right atoms. Separated charges are a demotion, not a disqualification.
